transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. I feel like I have to keep doing the same checks and routines over and over to make sure my wife is safe, and it’s taking up my whole day. It has gotten to the point where I am just completely exhausted and don't know what to do.
Can you describe what these checks and routines involve, and do you feel you have to do them to prevent something bad from happening?

I have to read her medication labels out loud, count each pill three times, and check the stove knobs and door locks in a precise order while repeating a silent phrase. I feel absolutely compelled to do this because I'm terrified that if I miss a single detail, she will stop breathing or end up back in the hospital, and it will be entirely my fault.
Do you feel anxious or distressed if you can't complete these routines, and does doing them provide only temporary relief?

Yes, I feel an absolute terror and even get sick to my stomach if I can't do them perfectly, because I'm terrified something catastrophic will happen to her. Completing the routines only gives me a few moments of relief before the doubts rush back in. Within minutes, I feel forced to start the whole process all over again.

The patient describes repetitive, ritualistic behaviors (counting pills, checking stove knobs and locks in a specific order, repeating a silent phrase) that are driven by intrusive fears (wife stopping breathing or returning to hospital) and a sense of compulsion to prevent harm. These behaviors cause marked distress, are not pleasurable, and provide only transient relief, which is characteristic of the specified condition. There is no evidence of symptoms suggesting other conditions such as mood disorders with secondary compulsions, psychosis, or anxiety disorders without obsessive-compulsive features.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits recurrent, intrusive thoughts about harm coming to his wife, which trigger compulsive checking and counting rituals performed to prevent perceived negative outcomes. These behaviors are driven by ego-dystonic obsessions and provide only transient relief, consistent with obsessive-compulsive disorder.
